I celebrate the little joys 🎉🍀, lift others up when they’re down 🙌💌, and never forget the moments that matter 📸💭. I am a friend who listens deeply 👂💬, supports tirelessly 🏋️‍♀️❤️, and loves without limits 🌍🔥. Even when life gets messy 🌪️💦, I stay grounded 🌳🕊️, patient ⏳🙏, and true to myself 🧩💞. Adventures excite me 🌄🚴‍♂️✈️, laughter fills my soul 😂🎶💃, and memories are treasures I keep forever 🏰💖📖. I shine bright 🌟💛, dream big 🌌🎨, and embrace every challenge 💪⚡, knowing that love, loyalty, and positivity 🕊️🌻 are the compass 🧭💖 guiding me forward 🌟🚀✨. I am loyal in thought 🧠💭, in word 🗣️💬, and in action 🏃‍♀️💨, holding close the people who matter most ❤️👨‍👩‍👧‍👦. I spread kindness 🌸💛 like sunshine 🌞🌻, share joy 🎊🎈 like confetti 🎉🌈, and stand firm 💪🛡️ even when storms 🌩️🌊 try to shake me. I cherish laughter 😂🎵, music 🎶🎹, and moments of peace 🕊️🌿, finding magic ✨🌌 in ordinary days 🌼🍃. I am a heart that loves fully ❤️🔥, a spirit that dreams endlessly 🌙🌟, and a soul that shines 🌈💫. I bring warmth ☀️🫂, hope 🌄💛, and unwavering support 🤝🌸, creating bonds that last forever ⏳💖. Do you want me to do that?To you all❤️ To Everyone Who Has Supported Me — Thank You. Sometimes the words “thank you” don’t feel big enough to express the kind of gratitude I carry in my heart. But today, I just want to pause and speak from that space — the one filled with appreciation for each and every one of you who’s been part of my journey, whether loudly or quietly. To my followers — the ones who’ve been here from the start, and those who just joined — thank you. Thank you for being present, for engaging with my content, for sharing it, for liking it, for commenting, and even for silently watching and supporting from a distance. Every click, every reaction, every message has meant more than you know. Some of you share my work without tagging me. Some of you recommend me in rooms I haven’t entered. Some of you defend me in spaces I’ll never see. Some of you speak my name with respect when I’m not even in the conversation. And even though I may never hear those words directly — I feel them. And I appreciate you. Then there are those of you who don’t follow me, but still show love. You don’t have to follow me to recognize my efforts, my growth, or my content. You support from the sidelines, and it still matters. Your support is just as powerful, just as appreciated, just as seen. Whether you’re a quiet observer or someone who occasionally engages — thank you. You’re part of the impact, and your energy adds to the momentum. Support comes in many forms, and I’ve learned to appreciate every version of it. Some people show love loudly, others do it quietly — both are valid. Both are beautiful. It’s easy to focus on numbers, algorithms, and growth — but none of that compares to the value of real support from real people. I don’t take it for granted. I know you don’t have to be here. I know you could scroll past. But you choose to be part of this space, this voice, this message — and that means everything. To those who’ve reached out privately just to say, “Keep going” — you have no idea how those words land. Some of you have lifted my spirit without even realizing it. You’ve reminded me why I do what I do. Why I share. Why I stay consistent. Your encouragement fuels my resilience. To those who have tagged their friends, told someone about my work, or shared my name in conversations — thank you. That kind of support is powerful. You’ve expanded my reach without asking for anything in return. You’ve amplified my voice simply because you believed in what I offer. That’s loyalty. That’s love. To those who’ve never met me, but believe in me — I see you. It’s one thing to support someone you know. It’s another to support a stranger based on what they share, how they make you feel, or what they stand for. You don’t owe me anything, and yet you give your energy, attention, and kindness. I’m grateful for that. I’ve grown so much — not just because of what I do, but because of the people around me who chose to believe in it. Because of those who didn’t just watch, but encouraged. Those who didn’t just consume, but connected. Those who didn’t just scroll, but stopped to say, “This matters.” Your support isn’t just about helping me grow — it’s a reminder that what I say, what I create, and who I am has value. That I don’t need to change or shrink or water down. That being myself is enough. And that kind of validation — the organic, unforced kind — is priceless. I’ve grown. I’ve glowed up — not just outside, but inside. I’ve unlearned the lies I once told myself and relearned the truth of who I am. I’ve walked away from what wasn’t serving me, even when it hurt. I’ve stood alone in rooms I once felt lost in, and found power in my own presence. I’ve cried. I’ve laughed. I’ve broken and rebuilt. Over and over. There were days I didn’t believe in myself. But *someone* did. Maybe it was you. Maybe it was someone who shared my post. Maybe it was someone who said, “You inspire me.” Those moments matter. You matter. I believe in divine timing now. I believe that everything and everyone comes into your life for a reason — to teach, to test, to heal, or to bless. And many of you, whether intentionally or not, have been a blessing. I’ve found encouragement in strangers, love in distant friends, and confidence in small milestones. That’s why I don’t take any of you for granted. Every like, every share, every “Keep going” has helped me keep *showing up*. And for that, I thank you — deeply and honestly. This journey has taught me that you don’t need to be famous to be impactful. You don’t need millions of followers to touch lives. Sometimes, just being real, being honest, being *you*… that’s enough. So, if you’re reading this, and you’ve ever thought, “They don’t notice me,” — I do. Maybe not always by name, but by energy. I feel the love. I see the support. I carry it with me. And this is not just about me — it’s about *us*. We’ve built something here. Something genuine. Something powerful. I hope that when you see my posts, you feel inspired. Not because I’m perfect, but because I’m proof that *healing is possible, growth is real, and dreams are valid.* I hope my words make you pause and reflect. I hope my heart reminds you that softness is strength. I hope my presence tells you: *you’re not alone.* And if you’re in a season of uncertainty right now — I see you. Keep going. It’s okay to outgrow people, places, and versions of yourself. It’s okay to take breaks. To protect your peace. To choose yourself. Growth can be quiet. Healing can be slow. But both are beautiful. As for me… I’m still becoming. I don’t have it all figured out. I’m still healing, still dreaming, still making sense of some parts of life. But I’ve made peace with that. I’ve stopped rushing the process. I’ve started trusting the pace. And most of all, I’ve started *trusting myself.* So, this post isn’t just gratitude — it’s a celebration. Of growth. Of connection. Of real people showing real love in a sometimes fake world. Whether we’ve known each other for years, months, or just a few scrolls — I thank you. If you’ve ever shared my words, laughed at my reels, related to my captions — I thank you. If you’ve ever whispered a prayer, told a friend, or simply sent good energy my way — I thank you. This space we’ve created together isn’t just about posts. It’s about purpose. It’s about healing, truth, love, and evolution. And I’m grateful to be on this journey with you. To those who support in silence: you’re just as powerful. To those who cheer loudly: you’re just as appreciated. To those who are just observing: welcome — I hope you find what you didn’t know you were looking for. As I continue to grow, evolve, and step into higher versions of myself, I promise to keep showing up — with truth, with heart, with purpose. And I hope you keep walking with me. From my heart to yours: *Thank you. Thank you. Do you want me to do that?To you all❤️ To Everyone Who Has Supported Me — Thank You. Sometimes the words “thank you” don’t feel big enough to express the kind of gratitude I carry in my heart. But today, I just want to pause and speak from that space — the one filled with appreciation for each and every one of you who’s been part of my journey, whether loudly or quietly. To my followers — the ones who’ve been here from the start, and those who just joined — thank you. Thank you for being present, for engaging with my content, for sharing it, for liking it, for commenting, and even for silently watching and supporting from a distance. Every click, every reaction, every message has meant more than you know. Some of you share my work without tagging me. Some of you recommend me in rooms I haven’t entered. Some of you defend me in spaces I’ll never see. Some of you speak my name with respect when I’m not even in the conversation. And even though I may never hear those words directly — I feel them. And I appreciate you. Then there are those of you who don’t follow me, but still show love. You don’t have to follow me to recognize my efforts, my growth, or my content. You support from the sidelines, and it still matters. Your support is just as powerful, just as appreciated, just as seen. Whether you’re a quiet observer or someone who occasionally engages — thank you. You’re part of the impact, and your energy adds to the momentum. Support comes in many forms, and I’ve learned to appreciate every version of it. Some people show love loudly, others do it quietly — both are valid. Both are beautiful. It’s easy to focus on numbers, algorithms, and growth — but none of that compares to the value of real support from real people. I don’t take it for granted. I know you don’t have to be here. I know you could scroll past. But you choose to be part of this space, this voice, this message — and that means everything. To those who’ve reached out privately just to say, “Keep going” — you have no idea how those words land. Some of you have lifted my spirit without even realizing it. You’ve reminded me why I do what I do. Why I share. Why I stay consistent. Your encouragement fuels my resilience. To those who have tagged their friends, told someone about my work, or shared my name in conversations — thank you. That kind of support is powerful. You’ve expanded my reach without asking for anything in return. You’ve amplified my voice simply because you believed in what I offer. That’s loyalty. That’s love. To those who’ve never met me, but believe in me — I see you. It’s one thing to support someone you know. It’s another to support a stranger based on what they share, how they make you feel, or what they stand for. You don’t owe me anything, and yet you give your energy, attention, and kindness. I’m grateful for that. I’ve grown so much — not just because of what I do, but because of the people around me who chose to believe in it. Because of those who didn’t just watch, but encouraged. Those who didn’t just consume, but connected. Those who didn’t just scroll, but stopped to say, “This matters.” Your support isn’t just about helping me grow — it’s a reminder that what I say, what I create, and who I am has value. That I don’t need to change or shrink or water down. That being myself is enough. And that kind of validation — the organic, unforced kind — is priceless. I’ve grown. I’ve glowed up — not just outside, but inside. I’ve unlearned the lies I once told myself and relearned the truth of who I am. I’ve walked away from what wasn’t serving me, even when it hurt. I’ve stood alone in rooms I once felt lost in, and found power in my own presence. I’ve cried. I’ve laughed. I’ve broken and rebuilt. Over and over. There were days I didn’t believe in myself. But *someone* did. Maybe it was you. Maybe it was someone who shared my post. Maybe it was someone who said, “You inspire me.” Those moments matter. You matter. I believe in divine timing now. I believe that everything and everyone comes into your life for a reason — to teach, to test, to heal, or to bless. And many of you, whether intentionally or not, have been a blessing. I’ve found encouragement in strangers, love in distant friends, and confidence in small milestones. That’s why I don’t take any of you for granted. Every like, every share, every “Keep going” has helped me keep *showing up*. And for that, I thank you — deeply and honestly. This journey has taught me that you don’t need to be famous to be impactful. You don’t need millions of followers to touch lives. Sometimes, just being real, being honest, being *you*… that’s enough. So, if you’re reading this, and you’ve ever thought, “They don’t notice me,” — I do. Maybe not always by name, but by energy. I feel the love. I see the support. I carry it with me. And this is not just about me — it’s about *us*. We’ve built something here. Something genuine. Something powerful. I hope that when you see my posts, you feel inspired. Not because I’m perfect, but because I’m proof that *healing is possible, growth is real, and dreams are valid.* I hope my words make you pause and reflect. I hope my heart reminds you that softness is strength. I hope my presence tells you: *you’re not alone.* And if you’re in a season of uncertainty right now — I see you. Keep going. It’s okay to outgrow people, places, and versions of yourself. It’s okay to take breaks. To protect your peace. To choose yourself. Growth can be quiet. Healing can be slow. But both are beautiful. As for me… I’m still becoming. I don’t have it all figured out. I’m still healing, still dreaming, still making sense of some parts of life. But I’ve made peace with that. I’ve stopped rushing the process. I’ve started trusting the pace. And most of all, I’ve started *trusting myself.* So, this post isn’t just gratitude — it’s a celebration. Of growth. Of connection. Of real people showing real love in a sometimes fake world. Whether we’ve known each other for years, months, or just a few scrolls — I thank you. If you’ve ever shared my words, laughed at my reels, related to my captions — I thank you. If you’ve ever whispered a prayer, told a friend, or simply sent good energy my way — I thank you. This space we’ve created together isn’t just about posts. It’s about purpose. It’s about healing, truth, love, and evolution. And I’m grateful to be on this journey with you. To those who support in silence: you’re just as powerful. To those who cheer loudly: you’re just as appreciated. To those who are just observing: welcome — I hope you find what you didn’t know you were looking for. As I continue to grow, evolve, and step into higher versions of myself, I promise to keep showing up — with truth, with heart, with purpose. And I hope you keep walking with me. From my heart to yours: *Thank you. Thank you. text: "Off the Cuff" - Markets were in "buy the dip" mode all day recouping nearly half of yesterday's drop even as there is uncertainty surrounding the tariffs that have been implemented since the Supreme Court is now in a hearing to discuss their validity. Even if the Supreme Court rules against them, there are still other ways they can be implemented. The Russell 2000 small cap index led the way higher today up 1.54%, the Nasdaq rose 0.65%, the S&P gained 0.37%, and the Dow advanced 0.48%. The VIX fell by over 5% back down to 18. Yields jumped up today after strong employment data with the 10-year yield closing up at 4.16%. WTI oil closed just below $60 per barrel. Eight of the eleven major sectors finished higher on the day. The sub-sectors outperforming the Russell today were Clean Energy, Blockchain, Semiconductors, Datacenters, and many more up 0.25-1.5%. Earnings of note after the close are from AppLovin, Arm Holdings, CF Industries, DoorDash, Dutch Bros, e.l.f. Beauty, Fortinet, HubSpot, Lyft, and Qualcomm. Earnings to watch for in the morning are from AstraZeneca, ConocoPhillips, Cummins, Datadog, DuPont, Granite Construction, Hyatt, NRG Energy, Parker-Hannifin, Ralph Lauren, Rockwell Automation, Tapestry, TripAdvisor, and Vistra. We will hear from a couple of more Fed governors during the day tomorrow. text: There’s a quiet debate that we’ve been having in rural America. It will never make the national news, and it won't affect most of the population, but it's leaving small towns looking for answers. • Immigration. • But not the kind you’re thinking about… ... stick with me. • See, we’re quick to talk about immigrants from other countries. • And truth be told, even when I don’t agree with the tone some folks take, I usually agree with the premise: If you’re going to come to America, learn the culture, understand the language, honor the heritage, respect the values, revere the flag, and become an American. • Its confusing to see people run from a broken nation just to demand America become the nation they ran from. • It hurts to see people wave a foreign flag that was worth leaving while taking advantage of the blessings found under this new one. • For generations, immigrants came here understanding the unspoken sacred rule: Becoming American meant letting something old die away so something greater could be born. • But here’s the undercurrent nobody wants to talk about… • Americans are doing the exact same thing to each other as you read this post. • Follow me. • Over the past number of years, there has been a mass migration, not from overseas, but from the big cities into the country. • People wanted space. Quiet. Kind neighbors. A place where the air felt cleaner, where the world felt slower. • And rural communities, generous as they always are, opened their arms wide. • These new immigrants moved into rural communities and talked about how much they loved the sound of driving on gravel roads, looking up into the sky and seeing stars, and how they enjoyed the feeling of soft soil under their feet. • But now? The murmurs are happening… • Now some of these same newcomers are annoyed …. • “The grocery store is too far.” “There’s nothing for the kids to do.” “We need more amenities, more activities, more, more, more.” • They left one world… then came here and started demanding the old world be rebuilt around them. • Tell me how that’s any different from an immigrant protesting America while waving the flag of the country he fled? • You moved here because it was different. You loved the charm. You loved the peace. You loved the simplicity. • But now that you live here, you have forgotten why you left "there". • You want a small town to behave like a big city while still pretending to be a small town? • Impossible. • So if you’re a transplant to a rural community, here’s the truth, spoken with love, and maybe a little annoyance: Learn the language of the land. Honor the history. Respect the sacrifices of the people who built it long before you arrived. And assimilate. • Growth is good when it’s wholesome. Everyone should be "pro wholesome growth". • But forced growth? • That’s how you kill the very spirit you came looking for. • Forced growth is how roots snaps instead of growing deeper. • So I encourage you, Breathe the country air. Embrace the slower pace. Appreciate the trade-offs. And let the community grow at the pace it was meant to. • Because if you liked the city life so much… … you should’ve stayed in the city.

Credit: Universal Pictures/ Courtesy: Everett *The Mummy*, Stephen Sommers’ rip-roaring reboot of the 1932 Boris Karloff classic, turned star Brendan Fraser into an action hero upon its release in 1999. The horror-comedy-action hybrid wasn’t a sure bet. The resurrection of the Universal monster franchise toiled in development hell for decades, with genre icons like George Romero and Clive Barker attached at various points. The studio wanted a low-budget horror flick, but Sommers pitched a swashbuckling, *Indiana Jones*-inspired take on the creature feature. The rest is ancient history. “I've always wanted to do a version of *The Mummy*,” he ** on its 20th anniversary. “I heard they'd parted ways with another writer-director… One of the first things I said was ‘Nobody wants to see a guy wrapped in bandages; they're going to laugh at it.’” History proved him right. The film earned over $400 million worldwide and received an Oscar nomination for visual effects. In the years since, there have been two sequels, a spinoff franchise, and a Tom Cruise-led reboot. text: #MARESBayanihanForHealth🪧Parents engage in crucial dialogue on School-Based Immunization at MARES Parents and guardians of Grades 1 and 4 learners gathered at the Manuel A. Roxas Elementary School Gymnasium on November 14, 2025, for an orientation on the upcoming School-Based Immunization Program led by the Department of Health (DOH) and the Local Government Unit. The session aimed to inform parents about the Measles-Rubella (MR) and Tetanus-Diphtheria (Td) vaccines for Grade 1 and the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine for Grade 4 girls, all scheduled for administration on December 4, 2025. Representatives from the Mini-Forest Health Center facilitated the discussions to ensure parents understood the importance, procedures, and safety of the immunization process. “This orientation is meant to empower you with knowledge,” said Ma’am Nancy B. Lopez, school principal, as she welcomed attendees. “We encourage you to listen, ask, and clarify anything that concerns your child’s health.” She emphasized that protecting children from preventable diseases begins with informed decisions and active participation of parents. The orientation proceeded with detailed presentations from health experts, addressing both the medical and procedural aspects of the program. Nurse II Karla Eunice C. Rondez explained that vaccines such as MR, Td, and HPV play a vital role in safeguarding children from serious illnesses, noting that Grade 1 learners will receive booster immunizations, while Grade 4 girls will be given HPV shots to prevent cervical cancer later in life. Meanwhile, Nurse II Kathrina Jasmin M. Orilla walked parents through the Parent’s Consent Form, stressing the importance of completing it accurately for the safety and documentation of the immunization process. The School-Based Immunization Program is a nationwide health initiative in partnership with DepEd, DOH, and local government units to increase vaccine coverage among school-age children. It aims to curb outbreaks of measles, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, and cervical cancer—diseases that remain significant public health concerns in the country. An open forum concluded the session, giving parents the opportunity to voice their concerns and seek clarifications before the December 4 immunization schedule. Despite uncertainties, many expressed appreciations for the school’s effort to guide families toward informed health decisions. With strengthened collaboration among the school community, health authorities, and parents, MARES continues to champion the well-being and protection of its learners.

text: Hey everyone — update from my little cocoon phase. 🦋 The last few weeks have tested me emotionally more than I expected. Lots of tears, lots of frustration, and way more restrictions than my impatient, hour-by-hour planner brain can handle. 😅 But even in the messy, slow-motion parts of this journey, I’m still here doing my best to kick cancer’s ass with sass and class. Medical snapshot: 💛 The cancer was removed and all lymph nodes were negative (huge blessing). 🖤 There were still some live cancer cells in the breast — super common in Triple-Negative — so I’ll still need radiation, oral chemo (Xeloda), and Keytruda. 💛 My mastectomy wounds aren’t healing they way we want and radiation can’t start until they do. So… plot twist: I’m having unexpected skin-grafting surgery tomorrow!🩺 My surgeon will remove the damaged tissue and use skin from my hip (bonus lipo, because why not at this point 🙃). Once that heals, I can start the next phase: radiation ➜ oral chemo ➜ onward. This whole experience has humbled me, stretched me, and slowed me down in ways I didn’t ask for… but I’m trusting the process. This is my cocoon — and I fully intend to come out of it stronger, wiser, and more beautiful than before. ✨🦋 Thank you for the prayers, messages, and quiet support. I feel it, and I’m so grateful. 💛
Happy Birthday Christian Merck Enriquez #MyApoSaPamangkin

text: ✨ FRONTERA SUMMER INTERNSHIP - STUDENT HIGHLIGHT ✨ Hi! My name is Raymond Alkakooz. I am a third-year student double majoring in Biomedical Sciences and Global Health. I aspire to be a physician for many reasons. From my journey from Iraq to Phoenix, to serving my community as a first responder, to seeing firsthand the health disparities that affect underserved populations, being a doctor has always been my calling. Witnessing the effects of gang violence, homelessness, and severe illness reinforced my duty to deliver the best care with empathy. Medicine, as a symbol, is incorruptible, enduring, and the purest form of human connection. This is why I pursued both degrees—to become a more well-rounded provider with biological knowledge and cultural inclusiveness. It has been an honor to work under Tomas Nuño, PhD, at the Arizona Prevention Research Center and the Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics at the University of Arizona. During the FRONTERA Summer Internship I researched quantitative and qualitative studies on HPV vaccine use, knowledge, and beliefs among U.S. southern border communities. I gained insights into vaccine hesitancy, cultural factors contributing to disparities, and how culturally tailored interventions can improve uptake. My favorite part of the program was the clinical experience. I externed as a population health technician at El Rio Health, a Federally Qualified Health Center. I conducted outreach for overdue A1C and diabetes retinopathy patients, helped providers prepare for appointments, and coordinated follow-ups with other clinics. A memorable includes receiving recognition from CDC scientific officer Rosalind Carter for my HPV research insights and participating in a clinic trip to deliver free medical care in Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, Mexico, with students from the University of Arizona College of Medicine - Tucson. Apply for the 2026 FRONTERA Summer Internship. Application closes on February 20. https://bit.ly/4oxn3Ru

text: Pfizer produces Premarin (conjugated estrogens) for feminizing hormone replacement therapy and Depo-Testosterone (testosterone cypionate injections) for masculinizing therapy. AbbVie manufactures Lupron Depot (leuprolide acetate), a GnRH agonist used off-label as a puberty blocker in gender-affirming care for youth. Eli Lilly has limited direct involvement in transgender-specific drugs, though market analyses include them in broader hormone therapy segments; their focus lies elsewhere like endocrinology for diabetes. These medications often require lifelong use, generating recurring revenue.

text: PRESS RELEASE World Cervical Cancer Day: NAPHDA and Pathfinder International Launch Free HPV Screening Initiative In an empowering initiative commemorating World Cervical Cancer Day, the Nasarawa State Primary Healthcare Development Agency (NAPHDA), in partnership with Pathfinder International, has launched a comprehensive free cervical cancer screening program for women and vaccination against the Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) for adolescent girls in Kwandere, Lafia. The program was inaugurated by Her Excellency Hajiya Salifat Abdullahi Sule, the First Lady of Nasarawa State, who made a passionate appeal for women to take advantage of this opportunity to protect their health. "Health is wealth. Let us help ourselves by utilizing this free cervical cancer screening provided by the state government and our partners for the well-being of our children," she urged. The First Lady emphasized the importance of regular cervical cancer screening and ensuring that young girls receive their HPV vaccinations. She encouraged women to seek medical attention promptly if they experience any symptoms, highlighting that early detection can save lives. Dr. Gaza Gowona, the Commissioner of Health, represented by Permanent Secretary Dr. John Damina, reaffirmed the state government's commitment to ensuring that vaccines and necessary medical equipment are readily available at designated treatment centers for the beneficiaries. He lauded the First Lady for her unwavering dedication to addressing health issues and praised the Executive Secretary of NAPHDA, Dr. Usman Iskilu Saleh, for spearheading the cervical cancer screening initiative. Acknowledging the First Lady's significant role in the success of previous health initiatives, including the measles and rubella vaccination campaign, the Executive Secretary noted that these efforts positioned Nasarawa State at the forefront of vaccine administration. He extended gratitude to the Kwandere community and their traditional ruler, Sangarin Kwandere, for their support. Fatima Maho, State Coordinator of Pathfinder International, expressed delight in the collaboration with the state government to promote awareness and encourage HPV vaccination. "My final call to you is to ensure you screen, educate, and vaccinate," she urged, assuring the community that subsequent screenings would follow in the coming year. Dr. Bosede Ezekiel, the World Health Organization (WHO) State Coordinator, speaking on behalf of other Partiners commended the state government for creating a supportive environment for partners to effectively assist the community. She praised Pathfinder International for their significant contributions to the cervical cancer screening and HPV immunization efforts. Marvellous Andrew, a beneficiary of the free medical outreach, expressed her gratitude towards the state government and Pathfinder International for launching the timely program, which would allow her to ascertain her cervical cancer status. This vital medical outreach initiative aims to screen over 100 women in the state, with immediate treatment options available for those who test positive for cervical cancer. Through this collaborative effort, NAPHDA and Pathfinder International are taking significant steps toward reducing cervical cancer risk and promoting public health in Nasarawa State. Signed Aminu Isiaka H (ANIPR). Information and Public Relations Officer NAPHDA 24TH NOVEMBER 2025.

It's been a long day. Kyle's scans are back. Forrest got scared but did okay once we convinced him we weren't there for him. It started out with us meeting with the Dr. Then we went to another part of the hospital for Kyle to have labs drawn, Kristin went with him while Forrest and I waited. They came out, we then had lunch and headed back to the oncology department. Then the news. My sister Sara was able to shade the mass that we're dealing with so it'll be easier to see. Kyle goes in this coming Thursday for his port, he'll then be admitted, then they start the chemo. He'll be there for 5 days, immune system completely suppressed but they're hoping he'll be home either before or on Thanksgiving day. This was like Dejavu all over again. The flashbacks I had were incredible. Kyle's mass was compared to "jello", it's a mass but it's not solid. We go in on Thursday, Kyle will have his port put in, then he'll be admitted. Chemo will start as soon as they're ready. My son will lose his hair. They're putting him on Ifosimide and Adriamycin in hopes to shrink or kill the tumor so it can be removed. As for the blood clot, he's to remain on Eliquis in hopes that it'll destroy the clot and his system will absorb it. They won't put in a graft to catch it because all that will do is create another clot. They're hoping Kyle will be home by Thanksgiving. He'll have to do this, like Forrest and me, every 3 weeks. One week inpatient, 2 weeks out, only where footrest and I come home, he'll stay. We're going to have to be extremely careful because he'll be immunocompromised. Even now, if Kristin and I take Forrest to the store, we hear a cough and we still rush Forrest as far away as possible in the other direction or we just leave. Kristin will stay with Kyle unless we trade off. Forrest and Kyle are the utmost priority. If Forrest will tolerate it, we'll stay with Kyle. We have a rule, we stay together, no matter what. Please pray for us, especially Kristin, she needs strength. We need her tested too Kyle Penquite Kristin N Lukemire-Penquite

The "X-Men" and "GoldenEye" alum talks all about "Forever Pour Toujours," her catchy single she recorded for the Dutch Netflix drama. Famke Janssen on Amsterdam Empire and recording that catchy 'Forever Pour Toujours' music video: 'It was tough' The "X-Men" and "GoldenEye" alum talks all about "Forever Pour Toujours," her catchy single she recorded for the Dutch Netflix drama. By Nick Romano Nick Romano is a senior editor at ** with 15 years of journalism experience covering entertainment. His work previously appeared in *Vanity Fair*, Vulture, IGN, and more. EW's editorial guidelines October 30, 2025 2:33 p.m. ET Leave a Comment Famke Janssen as Betty Jonkers on 'Amsterdam Empire'. Credit: - Famke Janssen is now, basically, a pop star, having recorded a professional single and music video for the Dutch Netflix drama *Amsterdam Empire*. - The actress talks about how "tough" it was to train in singing and dancing to pull it off. - "Betty is so unapologetically who she is," she says of her character. "Pour toujours, pour toujours / Forever pour toujours." The song is such an earworm, you'll likely hum it to yourself in the days after watching Netflix's *Amsterdam Empire*, a new Dutch drama starring Famke Janssen. The actress of *X-Men*, *Taken*, and *GoldenEye* portrays Betty Jonkers, marking her first time acting in Dutch since leaving the Netherlands to pursue modeling in her teens. Story wise, this ex-pop diva is out to steal her former husband's thriving marijuana coffee shop business after he left her for a younger woman he impregnated. Among Betty's claims to fame is a hit 1990s single called "Forever Pour Toujours." Janssen and Netherlands-based musician Palmbomen (a.k.a. Kai Hugo) professionally recorded and released the song through Netflix music. The star then also shot a music video. "Isn't it so catchy? It's hilarious, I know," Janssen tells **. "While we were filming, I was being trained for singing and dancing to make the video. And I kept pushing it, going, 'I'm so busy. Can we do it at the end of the shoot?' I thought, 'I need more time.' I love to dance. Trust me, it's one of my hobbies, but I've never been trained." Betty Jonkers (Famke Janssen) rolls up to the Amsterdam Music Awards on 'Amsterdam Empire'. She also doesn't consider herself a professional singer, even though "Forever Pour Toujours" is now on Apple Music and Spotify. She remembers, however, singing karaoke with the cast of *X-Men*, including James Marsden, who played Cyclops to her Jean Grey and previously commented on his costar's "beautiful" singing voice. Janssen remembers being in Tokyo with Marsden and his wife, Lisa Linde, where they would hit the karaoke bars. "I'm not speaking out of turn, she knew this: She had a terrible voice, he had the most incredible voice," she recalls. "They would do duets together and stuff like that. It was hilarious. But I've always been incredibly intimidated by singing." Famke Janssen details her struggles with fame: 'The press always wins' James Marsden calls 'Avengers: Doomsday' return a homecoming to 'X-Men' role She worked with choreographer Vincent Vianen, whom she describes as "meticulous" with the '90s-inspired movements. "It was tough. He had to be tough on me and he had to be very strict and firm," Janssen says. "I practiced. All day, whenever I was on set, people would see me in the background doing small moves." The Running Man was one such dance move she had to learn, since the video took inspiration from '90s hip-hop. "We started doing it on a slower speed in the beginning," she remembers. "Just try to do the Running Man. Do it at normal speed and then do it at the speed of the song ["Forever Pour Toujours"]. It was a challenge, but I did it." Famke Janssen on 'Amsterdam Empire'. The tone of *Amsterdam Empire* is an enjoyable concoction of *Breaking Bad*-esque drama (instead of blue meth, it's weed) but also *Real Housewives*-level camp. In one of her more soapy, theatrical moments, Janssen's Betty arrives by boat to the Amsterdam Music Awards to upend a big work moment for her ex's new lover. Nico Moolenaar, Bart Uytdenhouwen, and Piet Matthys created *Amsterdam Empire*, which Janssen also executive produces with Moolenaar. She says they were very specific in terms of the sought-after vibe. Janssen saw the character as a celebrity who believes music was a big part of her life once upon a time, even though it was a relatively small component in reality. "Betty is so unapologetically who she is," Janssen describes, "claiming space, asking for attention, dressing big, all of that. It's not at all the way I am in life. Just because of the fact that she was this one-hit wonder and she can't quite let go of it, there is that larger-than-life campy aspect to her personality, but I wanted to ground it in reality." ***Get your daily dose of entertainment news, celebrity updates, and what to watch with our EW Dispatch newsletter.*** Technically, Betty isn't a one-hit wonder. Janssen confirms she recorded multiple songs for *Amsterdam Empire*. "They kept throwing things at me, like, 'Did you wanna go to the studio?' And I go, 'Sure! Let's do it.'" Look out for that album release! *Amsterdam Empire* is available now on Netfllix.** Original Article on Source Source: "EW TV" Read More Source: TV #ShowBiz #Sports #Politics #Celebrities #Lifestyle November 01, 2025 at 10:01AM via @ALPHA MAG

text: She had 12 children and a PhD—when widowhood threatened to end her career, she revolutionized how America worked, one brilliant insight at a time. Most people see problems. Lillian Moller Gilbreth saw systems waiting to be perfected. Born in 1878 in Oakland, California, Lillian was the eldest of nine children—shy, brilliant, and hungry for knowledge in an era that told women their minds were decorative. Her father believed college was wasted on daughters. She proved him spectacularly wrong. By 1900, she had graduated from UC Berkeley. Then earned a master's in literature. Then, in 1915, she completed her PhD in psychology from Brown University—becoming one of the first women in America to earn a doctorate, at a time when most universities wouldn't even admit women. But Lillian didn't pursue psychology to analyze emotions. She wanted to understand human motion, efficiency, and dignity in work. She married Frank Gilbreth, a self-taught engineer as restless and innovative as she was. Together, they became pioneers of motion study—the science of making work faster, safer, and more humane. While Frank timed workers with stopwatches, Lillian watched their faces, their posture, their exhaustion. She asked the question few male engineers considered: Can work be made kinder? They filmed workers performing tasks frame by frame, identified inefficiencies, and created "therbligs"—17 fundamental motions that comprise all human labor. Their methods transformed factories, hospitals, and eventually homes across America. They wrote books, lectured internationally, and raised twelve children. Their household became a working laboratory—later immortalized in the book and film "Cheaper by the Dozen." Then, in 1924, tragedy struck. Frank died suddenly of a heart attack at age 55. Lillian was 46, with eleven children still at home and a career the industrial world refused to recognize without her husband's name attached. Clients canceled contracts. Factory doors closed. The engineering establishment dismissed her—woman, widow, mother—as unqualified. She could have retreated into grief and motherhood. Instead, she reinvented herself. If men wouldn't hire her for their factories, she would redesign their world anyway—starting with the spaces they'd never bothered to study: homes. Lillian interviewed over 4,000 women to understand their daily labor. What she discovered was revolutionary: kitchens were designed by men who had never cooked a meal in their lives. So she redesigned them with scientific precision. She pioneered the work triangle concept and advocated for optimal counter heights based on human ergonomics. She created the mobile workstation and pushed for better-designed kitchen tools that reduced repetitive strain. She studied how homemakers moved through their days and eliminated thousands of unnecessary steps. Her insights influenced refrigerator design, including interior organization. While specific inventions like the foot-pedal trash can are sometimes attributed to her (though documentation is unclear), her broader impact is undeniable: she transformed domestic work from invisible drudgery into a field worthy of engineering excellence. But Lillian's legacy extends far beyond kitchens. In 1935, she became the first female engineering professor at Purdue University. She advised multiple U.S. Presidents on workplace efficiency and rehabilitation. She consulted for General Electric, Macy's, and Johnson & Johnson. During World War II, she helped design workspaces accessible for disabled veterans. She worked into her eighties, earned over 20 honorary degrees, became the first woman elected to the National Academy of Engineering, and received the prestigious Hoover Medal for distinguished public service. Her philosophy was elegantly simple: "Good design should serve people. Efficiency should reduce suffering, not increase it." Lillian Moller Gilbreth didn't just study work—she humanized it. She proved that engineering without empathy is incomplete. That efficiency means nothing if it breaks the people performing the labor. That a woman with a PhD and twelve children could reshape American industry precisely because she understood both intellect and care. She was called "the mother of modern management" and "the first lady of engineering." But perhaps her greatest achievement was this: she refused to let the world's limitations become her own. When doors closed, she built new ones. When her expertise was dismissed, she found new problems to solve. When widowhood could have ended her career, she made it her launching point. Lillian Moller Gilbreth had 12 children and a brilliant mind—and she used both to prove that genius doesn't require choosing between family and achievement. It requires refusing to accept that you must.

text: Healthcare in costs in America is a tragedy 🤬🤬🤬🤬🤬 A U.S. government study found that in 2022, U.S. drug prices were on average ~229 % of Canadian prices (i.e., Canadian prices were about 44 % of what Americans paid) for the same drugs. Another review noted that for brand-name drugs, U.S. prices can be ~3 to 4 times higher than in Canada (or higher, depending on the specific drug). For example: Eliquis (a blood thinner) costs in the U.S. ~$1,668 for 180 tablets, while in Canada the lowest listed price was ~$370. Jardiance (for diabetes) cost ~$1,845 in the U.S. for 90 tablets versus ~$290 in Canada. An analysis found that Rinvoq (for Crohn’s/ulcerative colitis) is ~$11,915 in the U.S. vs ~$1,749.95 in Canada — roughly 7× the Canadian price. ⚠️ Examples of drugs with large U.S.–Canada price gaps Eliquis: ~4.5× higher in the U.S. vs Canada. Jardiance: ~6×+ higher in the U.S. vs Canada. Rinvoq: ~7× higher. In a broader list: Latuda (an antipsychotic) 90 tablets cost ~$4,628 in U.S., ~$520 in Canada (~89 % cheaper in Canada). Synthroid (for hypothyroidism) cost ~$114 in U.S. vs ~$44 in Canada (≈ 160 % higher in U.S.) in one older study. 🧠 Why does this happen? Canada uses government regulation and negotiation to constrain prices for patented drugs; the U.S. historically has fewer nationwide restrictions on drug manufacturer pricing. Brand-name drugs (patented) show the largest price gaps; generics often have smaller or even reversed differences. A study found that in 2017 the U.S. spent US $2,497 per person on health-care administrative costs, compared with US $551 per person in Canada. That’s more than 4× the Canadian per-capita amount. The source pointed out that if the U.S. reduced administrative costs to Canadian levels, it could potentially save over US $600 billion annually. Interpretation: A large chunk of U.S. spending is not directly care for patients, but overhead, billing, management, insurer profits, etc. 🔍 Example 2: Overall Spending and Payments to Providers The U.S. spends roughly twice as much per person as “peer” countries (including Canada) when it comes to health care. Much of the difference comes from higher payments to hospitals, physicians, and higher prices for services — not necessarily more services. For example: A source reports that the U.S. was spending ~16.8% of GDP on healthcare vs Canada’s ~10.8% (in one comparison) with the U.S. per-person cost at ~US $10,948 vs Canada ~US $5,370. 🔍 Example 3: Drug Pricing & Provider Mark-Ups While this example is more indirect, a recent report by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) found that U.S. pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) marked up prices of specialty generic drugs by thousands of percent between 2017-2022, leading to multi-billion-dollar gains. Higher negotiated prices, mark-ups, and less regulation in the U.S. contribute to higher profits in the supply chain. 🔍 Why This Shows Higher Profits (and Costs) If administrative/overhead costs are dramatically higher in the U.S., that means a larger portion of healthcare dollars is going to management, insurers, bureaucratic functions, profit margins — rather than directly to clinical care. Higher per-person payments to hospitals and physicians suggest that U.S. providers can charge (and are paid) more for the same or similar services. Higher drug mark-ups and profit-oriented structures in the U.S. supply chain mean more of the spending ends up as profit (or margin) rather than being passed on in lower consumer/patient cost. text: This isn’t the post I was hoping to write. These past weeks have been the hardest of my life so far. There were moments when I wasn’t sure I would reach this point — but your love carried me. Every one of you. My labs and degree of mucositis won’t allow me to safely get my final dose of A/C today. So Keytruda only. This is all part of the ride with metastatic cancer. We are hoping for A/C next week so I can stay on track for my surgery on Dec 10th. I want to thank @monica.kleinman and @christinexhall, who have been my constant caregivers. These remarkable humans did not step away from their lives to support me — they held everything at once: their families, many obligations, full-time jobs, graduate school, and me, along with all that this journey has required. Between them, they have been at every appointment, every transfusion, every chemotherapy session, and have cared for me nearly every day in between. Here’s to the caregivers — those who take on the hardest role. Please take a moment to check in on the beautiful humans who carry it all. Surround them with love and care; they need it, too 🩷🩷 #triplenegativebreastcancer #brca1 #metasticbreastcancer #caregivers

text: Lab Readiness: Positioning the Laboratory for Success in Molecular Testing This session is designed to foster collaborative problem-solving around laboratory readiness for molecular biomarker testing. Faculty composed of expert pathologists and molecular laboratory professionals will guide participants through a series of real-world case-based challenges and structured small-group discussions, focusing on issues such as test selection, validation, quality assurance, and regulatory compliance. Attendees will leave with actionable insights and peer-informed solutions they can bring back to their own practice environments. This session is supported by an independent educational grant from #AstraZeneca Pharmaceutic

text:
The Alzheimer's Defence Protocol Is HERE — And It’s NOT What You Think 

For decades, they told us Alzheimer’s was a mystery. A life sentence. An unstoppable force.

But what if we’ve been looking at it all wrong?

Renowned neurologist and neurodegenerative disease expert, Dr. Dale Bredesen, pulls back the curtain in a powerful new discussion. The key isn’t a single magic bullet—it’s a personalized, supplementary defence system.

“Supplements aren’t a cure for Alzheimer’s—of course they aren’t. They are, by definition, supplementary,” Bredesen begins. “But when you understand the root cause of cognitive decline, you can target your defence with precision.”

The paradigm is shifting. It’s not just about amyloid. It’s about why the amyloid is there.

Are you a “vasculopath” with underlying vascular issues? Your protocol will look different from someone battling Lyme disease or mycotoxin exposure.

So, what’s in the arsenal?

Bredesen highlights critical supplements that form the foundation of a robust cognitive defence:

- Omega-3s: Shown in multiple publications to support an anti-inflammatory state and, crucially, resolution of inflammation.

- Ginkgo Biloba: A classic for enhancing blood flow—powerful when combined with an overall cognitive optimization plan.

- Curcumin: Not only a potent anti-inflammatory but also binds and interacts with both amyloid and phospho-tau.

- Propolis: Another powerful anti-inflammatory agent.

- Resolvents (like SPM Active): Developed by Harvard’s Prof. Charles Serhan, these specialized pro-resolving mediators actively resolve ongoing inflammation.

- Magnesium L-Threonate: Developed by MIT researchers, this form is particularly effective for supporting brain health.

- Melatonin: Beyond sleep, it’s often low as we age and has noted anti-cancer effects at higher doses.

- Taurine & Creatine: Support muscular status and help tone down the sympathetic nervous system for better vagal tone.

- Vitamin D: A critical foundational piece for countless.

But Bredesen issues a critical warning: Do NOT take these willy-nilly.

“The problem with Alzheimer’s has been that people have been treating it blindly… We can now look much more deeply. We can determine why each person has the problem.”

The future is targeted. The future is personalized. The future is understanding that supplements like Bacopa, Ashwagandha, and Shankhpushpi can be powerful tools—when you know why you’re using them.

The era of passive acceptance is over. The era of strategic, intelligent defence is here.

It can handle heavy apps, high-resolution media editing, and demanding games effortlessly. In contrast, the iPhone 17 Pro Max runs on Apple’s A19 Pro chip, which leads in single-core CPU performance and optimized software integration. This makes the iPhone slightly superior for raw processing speed, gaming efficiency, and long-term software optimization. Both devices offer large storage options, with the S24 Ultra supporting up to 1 TB, and the iPhone 17 Pro Max up to 2 TB, catering to power users who store large media files or apps. Display & Design: Both phones feature large displays with high refresh rates. Samsung emphasizes versatility, AI-assisted image enhancement, and zoom capabilities. The iPhone 17 Pro Max has a triple 48 MP camera system with wide, ultra-wide, and telephoto lenses, prioritizing computational photography, color consistency, and video recording, including ProRes formats and cinematic features. text: I just want to start by saying a huge thank you to all of you who've been speaking out, sharing your thoughts, and holding strong to what you believe. Your voice and efforts are truly making waves and looks like the district is starting to back off a bit, explaining that things like Transgender Awareness Week are just for info and not something they're pushing or celebrating in our schools. It's a positive move, don't get me wrong, but honestly, they shouldn't have put those kinds of social issues on the calendar to begin with. Topics like this are the responsibility of parents to teach their children about at home, with no place in our public school system. It seems like they're trying to ease the tension from all the feedback, but it doesn't undo the mix-up and frustration it sparked. Our kids' schools need to be all about learning, feeling safe, and coming together. I hope the board will hold the Superintendent and folks involved accountable tonight. I'll be there at tonight's school board meeting, 5:30 PM at 125 N. Boundary St. in Manning and I'd love for you to come along too. It's so important for them to see us all, to feel our shared commitment, and to know we're in this together. On that note, though, the district still hasn't touched on my other concerns about Superintendent Dr. Shawn Johnson, like those sketchy contract extensions and other lingering problems we've been talking about. We deserve real answers and accountability... no more brushing things aside. As a Christian and someone who's blessed to serve our community, I feel deeply that we have to live by God's truth. Like in Matthew 6:24: "No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other." We can't try to please everyone by blending worldly ideas with what the Bible teaches. God gives us that inner wisdom discernment to spot what's true to His word, and we've got to lean on that. This isn't about pushing anyone away or being unkind. The Bible tells us to love our neighbors like we love ourselves, and I believe that with all my heart. But real love doesn't mean we have to go along with or promote things that go against God's plan. Folks who say you need to buy into this stuff just to be "nice" are missing the point. We can absolutely be kind, caring, and welcoming to everyone while staying true to our faith and not endorsing what doesn't align with it. That's where genuine compassion comes from. It's about lifting each other up and safeguarding our kids and community without giving in. Let's keep lifting this up in prayer, staying connected, and pushing forward for what's best. Hope to see you tonight!

text: At last night’s Township Council, the Mayor and Council presented a proclamation to Bristol Myers Squibb, honoring their support for the P.O.W.E.R. (Proactively Orchestrating Ways to Empower and Restore) Youth Mentoring Program. The Township Council approved a $20,000 grant from Bristol Myers Squibb for the P.O.W.E.R. initiative at the meeting. Kenneth Freeman, Corporate Security Senior Manager at Bristol Myers Squibb, accepted the proclamation. “I think the challenges for kids are really difficult so as long as we can we will continue to support the program,” he said. Freeman was joined by Councilman Alvin Rich, who is a mentor at North Brunswick Township High School, Detective Adrian Ailey, P.O.W.E.R. facilitator Tangie Cobb and North Brunswick Township High School P.O.W.E.R. coordinator Altagracia Ruiz. “P.O.W.E.R. is a great program for our school and beyond,” Councilman Rich said. “I look at the young people who entered in P.O.W.E.R. when we first started and looking at them now makes me smile so much just to see all the positive work that is being put in.” Det. Ailey said that over the course of the program, P.O.W.E.R. has received a total of $75,000 from Bristol Myers Squibb. The North Brunswick Township Police Department and North Brunswick Township Board of Education have partnered to facilitate the P.O.W.E.R. Initiative components: P.O.W.E.R ‘U’; P.O.W.E.R.: H2H – Hope2Heal and P.O.W.E.R. Afterschool at North Brunswick Township High School and North Brunswick Township Middle School. The P.O.W.E.R ‘U’ Summer Program supports incoming high school Freshman and the P.O.W.E.R. H2H – Hope2Heal Program is dedicated to student diversion and restoration during the school year, and P.O.W.E.R. Afterschool is a bi-weekly club dedicated to continuous student engagement, leadership practice and community outreach. Thank you Bristol Myers Squibb for your generous support to this important community program!

11/23/2025...I know that this is very early, especially for me, who has only decorated earlier than Thanksgiving night less than a handful of times in 71 years, but I'm still crying numerous times a day...sometimes in delirious JOY that my husband is still here, sometimes in overwhelming frustration in being SO overtired that I cannot even catch my breath, and still, occasionally, because I still watch him sleep, just to be sure that he's still BREATHING. I'm sure that you remember doing that over your newborn. I never dreamed that I'd do that over my husband, but here we are. It doesn't mean that I doubt God. That's the one thing I've never done, not ever, not once, since I committed to Him as a very young teen. But even the most glorious human beings in the world sometimes are taken before it's what we humans consider his or her time. God doesn't promise us that we'll have each other for all of our years together here on earth. He promises to be with us, no matter what happens, and I know that to be true. I can't imagine going through this without Him, but I, too, can't imagine seeing a perfect sunrise (or sunset) without Him, nor hearing a baby giggle, nor see the "light" go off in a child as they finally understand what has been being taught to them...I can't imagine one single moment of life without Him in it! His guidance, His comfort, His chiding when needed...I can't imagine life without Him. As you navigate your way through this Season of Love, I truly, with all my heart, pray that you have Him holding you, wrapping you in His love (and all that goes with His unconditional love), every single moment of every single day of your lives. We both thank you, from the bottom of our hearts, for the prayers that you've so diligently said for Ken through this journey that we've been on since June, and that ramped up SO much when he was admitted first to UMMC, then transferred to Buffalo General. He was admitted on 10/16, surgery (postponed due to him taking Eliquis in UMMC, which was the right call to treat what they had information about - AFib) was 10/27, and he was released on 10/31, a total, including partial days for admission and release, of 16 days. Your prayers during that time, and every day since he returned home, have been priceless. THANK YOU SO MUCH!!!!!!!!!! We can never repay you for your kindness, but we DO hope that you know just how much we appreciate you for your selflessness.

text: Ten years ago today — November 1, 2015 — I was assigned to my very first Business Intelligence (BI) project. That moment marked the real kick-off of my career in the Data Management field. I was 27 years old, working at ITWorx, when I got the opportunity to join an on-premises BI project for Pfizer. I was still a junior back then — eager, curious, and NERVOUS — but that project became the foundation of everything that followed in my professional journey. Back then, all my knowledge was purely theoretical. No SQL. No Data Warehousing awareness. Didn’t even know what ETL stood for or how it was applied. Not to mention OLAP Cubes, Reporting Tools, and all the rest. I still remember the day I was asked to write my first SQL command. It was on that same project — when the Country Manager asked me to run a sanity check on some data. And I thought to myself: “Oh God, he’s gonna find out that I’m a fraud.” I honestly don’t know how I powered through that phase. I just vividly remember spending days and nights reading about database design, ETL tools, reporting, and data architecture — trying to connect theory to reality. But there was a learning curve — and it paid off. That project became the stage for some of my proudest early achievements. During my 2.5 years at Pfizer, I optimized the data lifecycle workflow (from source systems to reporting tools), reducing refresh time from 14 hours to just 2 hours. Applied a manual MDM solution across multiple major systems. And supported reporting across the entire AFME region (Africa & Middle East). I consider myself lucky to have started my BI career when the BI was truly traditional and end-to-end — before heavy specialization. I got to do it all: Data Architecture, Data Modeling, ETL, Data Quality, BI & Analytics, Insights, and even a little bit of Data Science. Later, when I shifted more toward the business side as a Business Analyst in Data Management, I discovered my true passion and soft spot — being the bridge between the business and the technical worlds, speaking each one’s language. That solid technical start as a BI Developer opened amazing doors for me — to work as Business Analyst at CIB Egypt, Teradata, and Banque Misr بنك مصر. And for that, I’m truly thankful. And above all, I also consider myself extremely lucky and blessed to have learned from some of the best in the industry: Nedaa Agami, Sherif Isaac, Amr Ashmawy, Amirah Elsabagh, Heba Zaied, Walied Ebrahiem, Ahmed Emad, Diaa El-Bagouri, Tamer ElHossiny, Sherif Anwar, Karim Khalifa, Shaimaa El-Gammal, Gihan Mahmoud, Ahmed ElKhayal, Omar Maher, Mike Bellhouse, and many many more. (I don't wanna forget anyone, and sorry if i did) Thank you all for shaping my journey and helping me grow. I’m genuinely grateful for every lesson, every challenge, and every opportunity that brought me here 🙏 Here’s to the next ten years — of learning, building, and sharing back with the community.

text: On a Day Like Today ~ November 23, 2021. HRH Charles, The Prince of Wales, currently known as HM King Charles III, visited Cambridge Market. While there he toured the market and spoke with traders while viewing their goods. The future King then visited Homerton College part pf the University of Cambridge where he met student ambassadors of the programs and heard about the College’s well-being approach. Lastly, he opened a new AstraZeneca research and development facility in Cambridge. As its largest research and development center in the UK, the center will have more than 2,000 people working across therapy areas and drug discovery and development once fully occupied. text: 📢 Children with #JIA are taking centre stage globally! 🌎 Cassie + Friends is honored to represent children and youth with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis in the groundbreaking UNIFIED Project—a €27 million international partnership funded by Horizon Europe and led by Erasmus University Rotterdam and Pfizer. text: WAIT… YOU DON’T GIVE IMMUNIZATIONS?” — A CONVERSATION THAT SHOCKED ME I heard something a while ago that honestly left me speechless. A woman confidently said she doesn’t give immunizations to her children because “it’s not good” and “they don’t do it in their family.” I didn’t even hear the rest, because my mind froze. In 2025, with all the information the world has given us… With all the children who have died from diseases we can prevent with a simple shot… There are still parents proudly avoiding immunization. And that scared me. Because the truth is simple: 👉🏽 The risk of not giving immunization is far greater than the risk of giving it. Diseases don’t ask for your permission before attacking a child. And prevention has always been kinder than cure. The same thing happened when I posted about HPV vaccination. A pastor dropped a comment saying the vaccine was “a lie from the pit of hell.” I deleted it… but it stayed with me. Because some people forget that others actually listen to them. Some people forget the weight their words carry. And some public voices speak before they research, leaving innocent people to carry the consequences. So today, I’m bringing this here as a reminder: 💥 Mothers, fathers, caregivers, immunization is not the enemy. Ignorance is. 💥 Vaccines save lives. Not stories. Not vibes. Not family traditions. Actual vaccines. If you’re unsure about any vaccine, ask questions. Talk to verified health professionals. Seek knowledge not fear. QUESTION OF THE DAY: Have you ever heard someone confidently share a health belief that shocked you? CALL TO ACTION: 🟣 Share this post. 🟣 Educate one parent today. 🟣 Let’s create a generation that chooses knowledge over fear. Because our children deserve better than unverified information.

text: BBC MEMO WRITER'S TIES TO US PHARMA & TECH GIANTS. HIS GOAL'S BEYOND! ■‘BBC bias’ memo was written by American pharma lobbyist ■A guest post from Sam Bright. Dr Julia Grace Patterson💙 Nov 16, 2025 'My name is Sam Bright – I’m an investigative journalist and Substacker focused on exposing the populist elite (especially Nigel Farage and his cronies). Julia has been kind enough to share her platform with me, so I can tell you a worrying and important story about the author of the memo that blew up the BBC this week. Subscribe to Sam's Substack SPOILER ALERT - NOT JUST ABOUT A CLIMSY BBC EDIT: 'You probably all know the key developments, but I will recap them quickly in case you haven’t been following the gory details. ■Last week, a critical review of the BBC’s editorial policies was leaked to The Telegraph. It revealed how Panorama botched an edit of Donald Trump’s speech in Washington DC on 6 January 2021. ■Regardless of how the speech was edited, Trump encouraged his supporters to march on the Capitol, which left 174 police officers injured and lawmakers fleeing for their lives. ■However, the Panorama edit was clumsy at best, carelessly stitching together different sections of Trump’s speech. It was shoddy journalism. This scandal has snowballed – with The Telegraph and other populist reactionaries mounting an aggressive campaign to defenestrate our public broadcaster (despite The Telegraph’s own extensive record of editorial f*ck-ups). The BBC’s director-general has resigned, as has the CEO of BBC News, while Trump is threatening to sue the corporation for $1 billion. BUT JUST WHO IS MICHAEL PRESCOTT? But let’s go back to the beginning. The memo that kicked off this whole journalistic psychodrama was authored by Michael Prescott under his former capacity as an external adviser to the BBC’s Editorial Guidelines and Standards Committee. ■He is reportedly friends with Robbie Gibb, the BBC board member widely considered to be a Tory sleeper agent within the corporation. As has been extensively documented, Gibb (appointed to the board by Boris Johnson) was the director of communications for Theresa May when she was prime minister. He has described himself as a “proper Thatcherite Conservative”. ■Aside from having questionable friendships, Prescott is a corporate lobbyist. ■He’s the managing director of Hanover Communications – and his clients make for pretty grim reading. ■Chief among them is the American Pharmaceutical Group, which represents 10 of the largest U.S. pharma companies with a presence in the UK: AbbVie, Amgen, Biogen, Bristol Myers Squibb, Incyte, Gilead, J&J Innovative Medicine, Lilly, MSD, and Vertex. ■Official records show that Hanover has lobbied the Labour government on behalf of these companies over the course of the past few months. At the same time – and perhaps with Prescott’s help – American pharma giants have been pressuring (bullying is possibly a more accurate description) the government to open up the NHS to these corporate healthcare predators. ■As reported by Politico last week, American pharma giants have threatened to leave the UK if the NHS doesn’t pay more for their drugs. Eli Lilly – another one of Hanover’s clients – has said that it wants to see “significant and sustainable” change in the NHS before restarting its investment in a biotech incubator project. This threat has been echoed by Trump, who appears to have successfully lobbied for the NHS to pay 25% more for American medicines – accusing other countries of “freeloading” on his country’s pharma sector. Indeed, Trump is Big Pharma’s biggest champion – despite its decades-long record of fleecing, exploiting, and sometimes killing the American public. Why? Money, of course. Pharma companies donated an estimated $5 million to his re-election campaign and several million to his inauguration ceremony. Like so many other toxic, corrupt industries, they’ve bought their way into the president’s good books. ■At the top of this list is Big Tech, which has an incestuous relationship with Trump, a man who has become a battering ram for the interests of Silicon Valley tech bros and their virulent algorithms. ■Who else is on Hanover’s client list? You guessed it – Big Tech companies. Prescott’s firm lobbies for Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta, Jeff Bezos’s Amazon, and Apple – all of which have given millions of dollars to Trump in one form or another. ■■This complicates Prescott’s role in the BBC saga. It could well be argued that his firm stands to benefit from destabilising the UK’s relationship with Trump, knowing that the UK government may seek to offer concessions to American industries in exchange for the president dropping his lawsuit against the BBC. ■■We don’t know these were Prescott’s motives (neither he nor Hanover responded to my requests for comment), but this story is certainly not the simple tale presented by the right-wing press, of an independent, impartial observer sharing his concerns about the BBC’s editorial failures. Rather, by virtue of his mega-money American clients, Michael Prescott has a lot of skin in this game – a fact that should be a lot more widely understood. Subscribe to Sam's substack ■I’ll be back in touch in a few days to update you with the most important political developments and news about the NHS- there is a *lot* happening, and it’s so important that everyone is informed. ☆☆☆☆☆ ■Read Dr Julia Patterson NHS ENGLAND IS BEING ABOLISHED - what do we know so far? text: ✨ Today I’m Thankful… Even in the Waiting ✨ Today is one of those days where gratitude and fear sit side by side — and somehow, both are real. We’re waiting to hear back from Dr. Parker after my mom’s case is presented to the Tumor Board. They’ll be reviewing her PET scan, discussing the CAR-T Cell treatment plan, and deciding whether Cytoxan should replace Revlimid. And yes… Mom is worried about relapse. How could she not be? But even in this heavy moment, I’m thankful. Thankful for every blessing we’ve received so far. Thankful for each day she wakes up with strength she didn’t know she had. Thankful for the doctors who are fighting with her. Thankful for the treatments that have kept her here with me. Thankful that she still laughs, still steps on that stepper, still believes in hope even when the fear tries to take over. My job today is simple: Keep Mom comfortable. Keep her confident. Keep her spirit lifted while we wait for answers. Waiting is the hardest part — the mind runs wild, the what-ifs get loud — but faith has carried us before, and I believe it will carry us again today. So I’m praying that everything falls into place, that clarity comes from the Tumor Board, and that whatever the next step is… it’s one that leads her toward more healing, more time, more miracles. One Spark at a time, One day at a time. One blessing at a time. And today, I’m grateful for all of them. Sending hugs and healing prayers to everyone 🙏 💖

【世界灣區經濟論壇2025-生物醫藥專題環節】 【對談環節 - 醫藥創新協作新格局】 團結香港基金、廣州粵港澳大灣區研究院、澳門基金會於11月3日共同主辦「世界灣區經濟論壇2025」。 生物醫藥專題的對談環節以「立足灣區 聯動世界—醫藥創新協作新格局」為題，並邀得RDPAC前執行總裁康韋作為對談主持，對談嘉賓包括香港大學臨床試驗中心執行總監游廣智，因美納全球高級副總裁兼大中華區總經理鄭磊，東陽光藥業首席科學官林凱博士，勃林格殷格翰高級副總裁、大中華區研發和醫學部負責人張維博士，香港科研製藥聯會主席、香港阿斯利康總經理吳珊及香港科研製藥聯會董事、諾華中國高級副總裁及香港總經理陳永興。 新聞稿：https://bit.ly/3LJzV8N 活動回顧：https://bit.ly/43cPxI0 【The Global Bay Area Economic Forum 2025 - Biopharmaceutical Session】 【Panel Discussion - A New Pattern of Collaboration in Pharmaceutical Innovation】 Our Hong Kong Foundation, The Guangzhou Institute of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and Macao Foundation co-hosted the “Global Bay Area Economic Forum 2025” on 3 November. The discussion of the biopharmaceutical session themed “Rooted in the Bay Area, Connecting with the World — A New Pattern of Collaboration in Pharmaceutical Innovation”, featured experts to share their insight, including Kang Wei, Former Managing Director of RDPAC, as the moderator; Henry Yau Kwong-Chi, Managing Director of HKU Clinical Trials Centre; Jenny Zheng, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Greater China of Illumina; Dr Lin Kai, Chief Scientific Officer of Sunshine Lake Pharma (HEC Pharm); Dr Zhang Wei, Senior Vice President of Head of Medicine of Boehringer Ingelheim Greater China; Shan Wu, President of HKAPI, General Manager of AstraZeneca Hong Kong and John Tan, Director of HKAPI, Head of Hong Kong & SVP of Novartis China, as the panelists. text: Michael Kenneth Williams (November 22, 1966 – September 6, 2021) was an American actor. He played Omar Little on the HBO drama series The Wire from 2002 to 2008 and Albert "Chalky" White on the HBO series Boardwalk Empire from 2010 to 2014. He earned Primetime Emmy Award nominations for his performances in the HBO television biopic Bessie (2015), the Netflix drama series When They See Us (2019), and the HBO series The Night Of (2016) and Lovecraft Country (2020). He had a recurring role in the sitcom Community from 2011 to 2012. He also had supporting roles in a number of films including Gone Baby Gone (2006), The Road (2009), 12 Years a Slave (2013), Inherent Vice (2014), and Motherless Brooklyn (2019). Williams was born in Brooklyn, New York City, the son of a Bahamian mother from Nassau and Booker T. Williams, an American, from Greeleyville, South Carolina, where his African-American family has deep roots. Williams was raised in the Vanderveer Projects in East Flatbush, Brooklyn, and attended George Westinghouse Career and Technical Education High School. According to a DNA analysis, he was descended partly from the Mende people of Sierra Leone. After getting into trouble as a youth, he enrolled at the National Black Theatre in New York City. Williams worked for Pfizer pharmaceuticals as a temp. However, inspired by Janet Jackson's Rhythm Nation 1814, he left school and quit his job, against the wishes of his family, to pursue a career as a dancer. During a year in which he was intermittently homeless, Williams visited record labels and dance studios looking for work. He got a job as a background dancer with singer Kym Sims, which led to more work appearing as a dancer in music videos and on tours with artists such as George Michael and Madonna, as well as some modeling work. He also choreographed Crystal Waters' 1994 single "100% Pure Love". Williams had a large facial scar he received in a bar fight on Jamaica Avenue, New York City, on his 25th birthday, when he was slashed with a razor blade. The scar became his signature feature, and resulted in offers to perform as a thug in music videos, and modeling opportunities with noted photographers like David LaChapelle. One of his first acting roles was alongside Tupac Shakur as High Top, the brother and henchman to Shakur's drug kingpin Tank, in the 1996 film Bullet. Shakur reportedly decided on Williams for the role after spotting a polaroid photograph of him in a production studio. Williams also served as the American Civil Liberties Union celebrity ambassador to the Campaign for Smart Justice. Williams' portrayals of openly gay characters was deemed to be revolutionary. Williams gained recognition as an actor for his portrayal of Omar Little in The Wire, which began filming in 2002. The character was based on Donnie Andrews along with other crime figures in Baltimore. Williams received the part after a single audition, at the encouragement of writer Ed Burns. He was told that the character was slated to appear in just seven episodes and expected him to be killed by the end of the first season. However, creator David Simon stated that they always planned to keep the character as part of the continuing ensemble should the show be renewed beyond one season. For his portrayal of Omar, Williams was named by USA Today as one of ten reasons they still love television. Omar was praised for his uniqueness in the stale landscape of TV crime dramas and for the wit and humor that Williams brings to the portrayal. Omar has been named as one of the first season's richest characters, a Robin Hood of Baltimore's west side projects. The Baltimore City Paper named the character one of their top ten reasons not to cancel the show and called him "arguably the show's single greatest achievement". In 2007, he was nominated for an NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Actor in a Drama Series for his role as Omar. Williams pursued the role because he was intrigued by Omar's contradictory nature. He felt Omar's popularity stemmed from his honesty, lack of materialism, individuality and his adherence to his strict code. He felt that the role has been a breakthrough in terms of bringing attention to him and getting further roles. Williams received both positive and negative reactions to Omar's homosexuality and felt that he was successful in challenging attitudes and provoking discussion with the role. In 2008, then-U.S. Senator Barack Obama cited The Wire as his favorite television show, and called Omar his favorite character. About Omar, Obama said, "That's not an endorsement. He's not my favorite person, but he's a fascinating character ... he's the toughest, baddest guy on the show." During his portrayal of Omar Little, Williams went by his character's name and developed a habit of smoking cannabis and an addiction to cocaine in 2004. Williams lived part-time in Newark, New Jersey using drugs, but sought help from a ministry in neighboring Irvington, which he credited for helping him during the production. Williams was found dead in his Williamsburg, Brooklyn apartment by his nephew on September 6, 2021. On September 24, 2021, the NYC Office of Chief Medical Examiner confirmed that Williams died of a fatal combination of fentanyl, p-fluorofentanyl, heroin and cocaine, and ruled the death as an accidental overdose. His private funeral was held at St. Stephen's Episcopal Cathedral in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania where his mother lives.

text: Bell: The point here is that, whatever new data is coming out on Covid vaccines, the public was systematically misled, misinformed, and lied to by our public health agencies. This is not controversial – they simply were. We can wonder at the lack of interest in the excess deaths in the vaccinated group over the unvaccinated in the 6-month Pfizer trial published in 2021, and the lack of any detectable benefit on mortality in the equivalent Moderna trial. We can wonder at the secrecy around the commitment of hundreds of billions of public funds in pre-purchase commitments, sometimes negotiated by text message, and how the people who did this are still in power. We can really wonder why there is so little solid data on overall mortality and disability of vaccinated versus unvaccinated people, when this is such an obvious thing for our governments to check. Human biology is complex and variable – lots of people (clearly) had plenty of injections and are (and almost certainly will be) fine. Lots of others probably will not be so fine. This is why, back in the days of medical ethics, we were supposed to be informed and given a choice. We really should wonder why that changed, and why doctors agreed to go along with it (such things have happened before).
